# Statistical Analyses and Results

## Initial Data Analysis

```{r ida-load}
data_path <- here::here("data", "processed", "clean_data.rds")
if (!file.exists(data_path)) {
  stop("Missing ", data_path, ". Put sales_data.csv in data/raw/ and run scripts/01_clean_data.R")
}
dat <- readRDS(data_path)
```

```{r ida-checks}
n_dup <- dat |>
  count(date, store_id, product_id) |>
  filter(n != 1) |>
  nrow()
n_na <- sum(is.na(dat$demand))
n_nonpos <- sum(dat$demand <= 0)
```

Before fitting the initial multiple linear regression model, we explore the structure of the dataset. Each observation represents a particular product at a particular retail store on a given day. The cleaned dataset contains `r format(nrow(dat), big.mark = ",")` observations across `r nlevels(dat$store_id)` retail stores and `r nlevels(dat$product_id)` distinct products, covering `r gsub(" 0", " ", format(min(dat$date), "%B %d, %Y"))` to `r gsub(" 0", " ", format(max(dat$date), "%B %d, %Y"))`, and each store-product-day combination appears exactly once (`r n_dup` duplicates).

The dataset contains 16 variables: nine numeric variables, six categorical variables (store, product, category, region, weather condition and seasonality), and one date variable. Although promotion and epidemic are stored as numeric variables, both are binary indicators taking values 0 or 1; `r round(100 * mean(dat$promotion))`% of the observations are promoted and `r round(100 * mean(dat$epidemic))`% occur during an epidemic.

```{r ida-summary}
dat |>
  select(where(is.numeric)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable") |>
  group_by(Variable) |>
  summarise(Mean = mean(value), SD = sd(value), Min = min(value), Max = max(value)) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE, digits = 2, caption = "Summary statistics of the numeric variables") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")
```

Daily product demand has a mean of `r round(mean(dat$demand), 2)` units and a standard deviation of `r round(sd(dat$demand), 2)` units, with observed values ranging from `r min(dat$demand)` to `r max(dat$demand)` units. There are `r n_na` missing and `r n_nonpos` zero or negative demand values, so zero-demand observations are not a concern in this dataset. Inventory level and units ordered exhibit substantial variability, and the standard deviation of units ordered exceeds its mean. Product prices and competitor prices have similar means and standard deviations, and discounts range from 0 to 25 with an average of `r round(mean(dat$discount), 2)`.

```{r ida-boxplots, fig.cap = "Boxplots of demand by product category"}
cat_stats <- dat |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(n = n(), Mean = mean(demand), Median = median(demand), SD = sd(demand))

ggplot(dat, aes(x = category, y = demand, fill = category)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Product Category", y = "Demand") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The demand distributions are right-skewed in all five categories, with most observations below 200 units and long upper tails containing many high outlying values. Groceries has the highest mean and median demand (`r round(cat_stats$Mean[cat_stats$category == "Groceries"], 2)` and `r cat_stats$Median[cat_stats$category == "Groceries"]` units) and the highest variability (SD `r round(cat_stats$SD[cat_stats$category == "Groceries"], 2)`), followed by Clothing (mean `r round(cat_stats$Mean[cat_stats$category == "Clothing"], 2)`). Furniture has the lowest mean and median (`r round(cat_stats$Mean[cat_stats$category == "Furniture"], 2)` and `r cat_stats$Median[cat_stats$category == "Furniture"]`) and the least variability (SD `r round(cat_stats$SD[cat_stats$category == "Furniture"], 2)`). The categories are also unbalanced, with `r format(max(cat_stats$n), big.mark = ",")` observations for Groceries but only `r format(min(cat_stats$n), big.mark = ",")` for Electronics. These differences in both center and spread suggest that product category is an important predictor and motivate checking whether the error variance differs across categories.

```{r ida-pairs, fig.cap = "Pairwise relationships (random sample of 2,000 rows)", fig.height = 4.5}
set.seed(4130)
ida_sample <- dat |>
  slice_sample(n = 2000) |>
  select(demand, price, discount, competitor_pricing, inventory_level)
ida_cor <- cor(ida_sample)

ggpairs(ida_sample, lower = list(continuous = wrap("points", alpha = 0.2, size = 0.5)))
```

To explore the relationships between demand and the quantitative predictors, we construct a scatterplot matrix from a random sample of 2,000 observations. Demand has weak positive correlations with discount (`r round(ida_cor["demand", "discount"], 3)`) and inventory level (`r round(ida_cor["demand", "inventory_level"], 3)`) and weak negative correlations with price (`r round(ida_cor["demand", "price"], 3)`) and competitor pricing (`r round(ida_cor["demand", "competitor_pricing"], 3)`). Price and competitor pricing have a very strong positive correlation of `r round(ida_cor["price", "competitor_pricing"], 3)`, which indicates potential multicollinearity, while the remaining pairwise correlations are weak. Demand, price, competitor pricing and inventory level are right-skewed to varying degrees, and discount takes only a few discrete values.

Overall, the initial data analysis reveals differences in demand across product categories, weak marginal associations between demand and the quantitative predictors, and potential multicollinearity between price and competitor pricing. All demand values are positive, which eliminates concerns regarding zero-demand observations.
